sections.title: The Umbrian Hills and Assisi
sections.intro: Umbria is a region in central Italy. It is characterized by hills, mountains, valleys and historical towns, such as Assisi, a World Heritage Site. Religious pilgrims have come to Assisi for centuries to visit the Basilica of San Francisco, where St. Francis is buried. Saint Francis founded the Franciscan religious order in Assisi in 1208. Assisi is also the home of the Basilica of Santa Chiara, where the tomb of St. Clare, the founder of the Sisters of the Poor, is located.  The Basilica of Maria Degli Angeli is located on the Umbrian plains near Assisi. Built between 1569 and 1679, it enclosed the Porziunculai (little church), the most sacred place for the Franciscans. sections.intro: Venice is located in northeastern Italy. It is situated on a group of 118 small islands that are separated by canals and linked by over 400 bridges. sections.title: Florence
sections.intro: Florence is a city rich in museums, churches and art galleries, as well as shops to purchase leather and gold. Highlights included the Cathedral with its beautiful Baptistery; the Santa Croce Basilica; the Uffizi Gallery; the Accademia where we viewed Michelangelo's David among other great statues and paintings; and the Piazza della Signoria.  Loggia dei Lanzi in Piazza Della Signoria, is an open air museum designed in the 14th century. Below the arches are dozens of statues including The Rape of the Sabine Woman 1583 AD., pictured above. This museum adjoins the Uffizi Gallery.  Piazza Della Signoria, was the center of Political life in Florence. The prominent Palazza Vecchio overlooking the square was the main symbol of civil power in the city, and the meeting place of the city council. Construction on the solid fortress began in 1299 AD.  Inside the Accademia Museum stands the original statue of David.

sections.title: The Colosseum
sections.intro: The Coliseum, also known as the Flavian Amphitheater, is in the center of Rome. It is oval in shape and built of Travertine limestone, tuff, and brick-faced concrete. It could hold 50,000 spectators. Construction began in 72 AD and was completed in 80 AD. It was a gift to the Roman people by the Flavian emperors for entertainment including gladiatorial combats and wild animal fights.

sections.title: St. Peter’s Basilica
sections.intro: Designed by Bramante, Michelangelo, Maderno, and Bernini, it is the most renowned work of Renaissance architecture and the largest church in the world. Construction was started by Pope Julius II in 1506 AD and completed in 1615 AD under Paul V. It is designed as a three-aisled Latin cross with a dome at the crossing, directly above the high altar, which covers the shrine of St. Peter.  Exterior door  St. Peter's Basilica

sections.title: Sistine Chapel
sections.intro: The Sistine Chapel is located in the Apostolic Palace, the official residence of the Pope. The chapel takes its name from Pope Sixtus IV, who restored it between 1477 and 1480. It is a place of both religious and functionary papal activities, including the papal conclave, the process by which a new pope is selected. Its fame lies in the many frescos that decorate the interior - most notably the ceiling of The Last Judgment by Michelangelo.

sections.title: York, England
sections.intro: No other city in northern England says medieval like York, a city of culture and historical wealth. The Romans built the city in 71 AD and the Vikings captured it in 866 AD. A circuit of 13th century walls encloses a medieval web of narrow streets. At its heart lies the immense York Minster. This modern tourist-oriented city has a myriad of museums, historical sites, restaurants, cafes and traditional pubs.  Since Roman times, The York City Walls have defended York and are England's most complete set of city walls. Made of structures built at different times, it has four main stone gateways known as "bars" and 34 towers. The walkway around the walls was a great way to see the historic sites of York.  The Abbey of Saint Mary's Manor was founded in 1155 as a Benedictine monastery. It was extensively damaged by fire in 1157, and rebuilt by 1294. King Henry VIII banned all monasteries in England in the 1530's and the buildings were converted to a palace for the King when he was in York. Gradually the abbey, which is located behind York University, fell into ruins.

sections.title: Touring Edinburgh Castle
sections.intro: Stone of Scone, also known as the Stone of Destiny (or Coronation Stone) is an oblong block of red sandstone. Legends of its origins date back to biblical times. A descendant of King Gathelus brought the Stone to Ireland and was crowned on it as king of Ireland. From Ireland, the Stone moved with the invading Scots to its home in Scone. The Stone remained in Scone until it was forcibly removed by English King Edward in 1296 and taken to Westminster Abbey. Every English monarch since 1296 has sat on the Stone for their coronation. On Christmas Day in 1950, the Stone was famously abducted from Westminster by a group of Glasgow students who brought it back to Scotland. The Stone was returned by the Stone-nappers the following April. In 1996, the Stone was returned to Scotland where it is kept today. The Coronation Chair was made to house the stone in 1301 and it was first used at the coronation of Edward II, and thereafter to crown all kings and queens of England.

sections.intro: We drove from Edinburgh to Stirling, Scotland where we toured Stirling Castle.  Stirling Castle is one of the most important castles in Great Britain. The castle was built in early 12th century, on a hill of volcanic rock. Its other buildings were added from the period 1490-1600. At the castle's heart is the Inner Close, a square formed by the King's Old Building, Great Hall, Royal Palace, Royal Chapel, and the gardens. The castle is surrounded by a heavy defense of walls, towers, gates, and artillery. It was very much a palace as well as a fortress. Several Scottish Kings and Queens have been crowned here including Mary Queen of Scots, in 1542. Many others were born or died here.  The Great Hall - Built for James IV around 1503, is the largest banqueting hall in Scotland. There are five ornate fireplaces, spiral stairways and a hammer- beam roof constructed from around 350 oak trees. In 1594, James VI held a banquet for the baptism of his son, Prince Henry. sections.title: Touring the Exterior of Notre-Dame Cathedral
sections.intro: Notre-Dame Cathedral is a medieval Catholic cathedral on the Île de la Cité. Built between 1163 (started during the reign of King Louis VII) and 1345, it is one of the oldest Gothic cathedrals in the world. The cathedral was consecrated to the Virgin Mary. Its use of the rib vault and flying buttress, its enormous and colorful rose windows, and an abundance of sculptural decoration set it apart from the earlier Romanesque style. Major components include its large historic organ and its immense church bells. The cathedral had its share of both glorious and tragic historical moments, including the crowning of Henry VI in 1431 and Napoleon in 1804. Notre-Dame sustained considerable damage to its roof and spire in a fire in April 2019. Restoration work was set to be completed in 2024.

sections.title: The Rijksmuseum
sections.intro: A Dutch National Museum dedicated to arts and history in Amsterdam. It was founded in the Hague in 1798 and moved to Amsterdam in 1808, where it was first located in the Royal Palace and later in the Trippenhuis. (The Trippenhuis is a canal mansion built in 1660-1662 for the wealthy weapons traders, Louis and Hendrick Trip.) The current main building was first opened in 1885. The museum has a total collection of 1 million objects, among which are masterpieces by Rembrandt, Frans Hal, and Johannes Vermeer.

sections.title: Heidelberg
sections.intro: While in medieval Old Town, we also walked the famous Old Bridge (Karl Theodor Bridge). The bridge crosses the Neckar River connecting the Old City with the eastern section. The twin towers were once part of the city wall and contained dungeons. Heidelberg's oldest bridge, it is an architecturally impressive landmark decorated with an imperious gateway, detailed sculptures, and a curious monkey holding a mirror. The monkey sculpture welcomed all to Heidelberg and was meant to remind those who crossed the bridge to look back and remember where they had come from. Local legend has it that rubbing the mirror brings good luck, rubbing the fingers ensures a return to Heidelberg, and rubbing the little bronze-cast mice brings fertility.  Art and Gin

sections.title: Havana, Cuba
sections.intro: Wednesday, April 10: We disembark our ship and meet up with our Excursion Guide who narrates as we explore historic Havana Cuba. A short boat ride across the bay takes us past the statue of El Cristo, an impressive 55-foot-tall statue of Christ sculpted in Italian Marble. We begin our walking tour through the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Old Havana, exploring the vibrant colors and people of this 16th century part of the city. Here, there are four main squares or plazas each offering its own unique characteristics, vendors, street performers and musicians. These include: Plaza de San Francisco de Asis (St. Francis of Assisi Square), Plaza de Armas, Plaza de la Catedral and Plaza Vieja.  Our first stop is Plaza de San Francisco de Asis which is a short distance from the docks. This Plaza, founded on June 2, 1628, is one of the oldest squares in Havana. Here we have time to see The Basilica of St. Francis of Assisi and numerous other historic buildings. Next, we visited Plaza de Armas with its many historic buildings, wooden street and street performers. The main highlight of this Plaza is the park with its beautiful palm trees and marble statues. Our Excursion Director then took us to visit the Fortaleza de San Carlos de la Cabana (Fort of St. Charles) complex that served in the defense of Old Havana back in the days of pirates and privateers. While here, we also saw a demonstration of cigar making. Our way back to Old Havana took us past El Capitolio (the National Capitol Building) and Obispo Street, in Central Park, the most populous street in Old Havana, with all of its vintage cars on display.

sections.title: Havana, Cuba (continued)
sections.intro: We enjoyed lunch at a local restaurant and then were entertained by the Retazos Dance Company. This performance was a part of our requirement to participate in a group people-to-people exchange for authorized travel to Cuba. This contemporary dance group is one of the most admired dance companies in Latin America. In the afternoon, we continued our tour by bus through Old Havana's streets and neighborhoods where we viewed local Cubans, their homes, shops, schools and vintage cars. As a part of our bus tour, we had photo opportunities at Plaza de La Catedral (Cathedral Square). Following the construction of the Cathedral in 1727, it became the site of some of the city's grandest mansions and numerous restaurants.  Our tour did not have time to visit Plaza Vieja, also known as Old Town Square. Here, Colonial buildings allowed residents in the early 16th century, a view of public demonstrations such as bullfights, processions and even executions. Today, the Square has many restaurants and bars. Our tour ended back at our ship. After dinner, we joined other cruise guests at the Piano Bar.

sections.title: La Sagrada Familia
sections.intro: La Sagrada Familia, meaning Holy Family, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The original architect, Francisco de Paula del Villar, had a plan for a Gothic revival church. Construction began in 1882 and Antoni Gaudi became involved in 1883. La Sagrada Familia was envisioned by Gaudi with a total of 18 towers; twelve dedicated to the Apostles, the others to the Four Evangelists, the Virgin Mary and Christ. At the time of Gaudi's death in 1926, less than a quarter of it was complete. It has a completion date of 2026, the centennial of Gaudi's death. The Crypt, the oldest part of the Basilica, is where Gaudi was buried. In November, 2010, La Sagrada Familia was consecrated and proclaimed a minor basilica by Pope Benedict Xvi.

sections.title: Mykonos, Greece
sections.intro: Walking Tour of Mykonos  We returned to Mykonos for a guided walking tour. Mykonos is a picturesque town with tiny streets, white houses and red roofed churches. It is one of Greece's most expensive islands after becoming a home to the jet set. We saw windmills dotting the landscape, to remind us that the island was once known for its agriculture. We viewed Little Venice famous for its narrow rows of colored fishing houses that sit at the edge of the sea. Originally the homes belonged to rich merchants. Little Venice is a hub of activity with shops and restaurants. We saw Paraportiani Church, which is actually five churches; four comprise the base and the fifth is built as the dome. After the tour, we walked the streets on our own past the many shops, boutiques and had lunch.
